messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Housekeeper
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 44

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drop Responsibilities: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers, Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Tyler had grown accustomed to the darkness that crept in every night. As a housekeeper at a busy hotel, he often worked late shifts and would return home under the veil of evening shadows. But despite his familiarity with nighttime, it still unsettled him. He couldn't quite explain why, but something about the absence of light made him feel vulnerable, like an invisible presence was lurking just out of sight. As a child, Tyler had been physically abused by one of his caregivers. The memories were hazy, but certain details lingered – the scratchy texture of the carpet in the room where it happened, the muffled sounds of children crying from elsewhere in the house. Whenever he encountered these triggers, the past came flooding back. At work, Tyler struggled to cope with the sound of kids crying. It didn't matter if they were just upset about a lost toy or having a tantrum; to him, their wails transported him straight back to that dreaded room. He would hastily excuse himself and retreat to a quiet corner, trying to collect his thoughts before returning to his duties. Tyler's way of dealing with these overwhelming memories was to disengage from reality altogether. When the emotions became too much to bear, he would drift off into a world of his own – a fantasy escape where the pain and fear didn't exist. It was a fleeting reprieve, but it helped him get through the tough moments. As time went on, Tyler started to notice that he was dropping responsibilities more often. He would call in sick or leave work early without explanation, simply because he couldn't face the world outside his apartment. His colleagues grew concerned about his reliability, and his manager began to question his commitment to the job. Despite this, Tyler felt compelled to avoid being alone with others whenever possible. It wasn't that he didn't trust them; it's just that he believed people could see right through him, into the depths of his painful past. He imagined they could spot the scars – not physical ones, but the invisible marks left by years of abuse and neglect. In those quiet moments when Tyler was alone with his thoughts, memories replayed like a perpetual film loop in his mind. The sounds, sights, and sensations came flooding back, transporting him to that traumatic event all over again. When this happened, he would shut down entirely – unable to speak or think coherently until the memory had receded. Tyler couldn't shake off the feeling of being an object rather than a person. It was as if he'd lost control over his own life, and everyone around him saw only a shell of who he truly was. Even more terrifying, though, was the constant fear that lurked beneath – a nagging suspicion that anyone could harm him at any moment. Sometimes, without warning, Tyler would relive the traumatic experience in vivid detail. It wasn't just memories; it felt like his body and mind were reliving every second of that awful event all over again. The physical sensations left him gasping for breath – a familiar but intense response to the perceived threat. Tyler's world had become one of heightened alertness, where potential dangers lurked around every corner. He couldn't relax in public or quiet spaces; his senses were perpetually on high alert, waiting for something, anything, that might signal another attack. This state of hypervigilance left him exhausted – a tiredness not just physical but emotional as well. One evening, after an especially grueling shift at the hotel, Tyler stumbled upon an article about PTSD support groups in his local area. It was then he realized how suffocating his situation had become. Something within him stirred; for the first time in years, he felt a glimmer of hope that things could change – that with help, he might finally begin to heal and reclaim control over his life. Tyler's eyes locked onto the phone number at the bottom of the page as if it held the key to unlocking his freedom. With a hesitant determination, he reached for his phone and dialed, the first step toward seeking help after years of suffering in silence.
